Another shot from outside the box as Arsenal’s defenders backed off, and the Greek striker found the bottom corner. What a first half for Brighton, Arsenal need to pull something out of the fire in the second half. Just before the goal, Saka had a chance after a deflected Odegaard shot.

Brighton’s second goal was an even better hit than their first. End-to-end football resulted in Kostoulas having space 20 yards from Arsenal’s goal. It’s another thumping low finish. Brilliant, breathless half of football by Brighton.

As half-time approaches, Arsenal have mustered just one shot on goal worth 0.03 expected goals. When they have moved the ball beyond Brighton’s press, they have not done anywhere near enough with it.

This fixture last season was especially bad-tempered, with the Brighton fans (and manager) repeatedly accusing Arsenal of time-wasting. The memories of that defeat are clearly still fresh in the minds of the Brighton supporters, who are roaring with rage at every perceived delay by the visitors, despite the fact that Arsenal are losing. The bad blood is adding to the intensity of the occasion.

Ipswich don’t play like a team that is short of confidence and quality. You might assume, if you haven’t seen much of them, that they are destined for a season of toil but there is definite quality with Gary O’Neill’s ranks, including Abdul Fatawu, who has been magnetic in drawing your eye to him. They might be a goal down but they are playing as if they are a goal in front.

Arsenal had just enjoyed a spell of control, but trail to a goal from one of the league’s in-form players. Gross whips a shot from just outside the box around Raya and in off the post.

Brighton have the lead at the Amex and it’s their captain, Pascal Gross, who has provided it. Superb long-range effort, in off the near post. On the overall balance of play, Brighton deserve that. It’s reward for their courage and willingness to go after Arsenal, rather than sitting back.

It took almost 20 minutes but Arsenal have found their feet in this game now. They are starting to find avenues through Brighton’s aggressive pressing and have made a few promising runs in behind, through Havertz and Saka. This is a high quality match.

No goals at the Amex, but Brighton are the team making the running, Arsenal struggling to play out from their own half and are yet to register a shot on goal.

Barry kept himself onside and turned the ball into the back of the net with his stomach. He did well to avoid a handball.

Bright start from Everton and they have the goal they deserve, albeit it came in fortuitous circumstances. James Tarkowski’s volley clattered into Thierno Barry and the deflection took it away from Christian Walton in Ipswich’s goal. Barry now has five goals for the season and, while he is raw, it’s an invaluable contribution.

A storming response to a bad night at Leeds from Newcastle, and it looks like being a long afternoon for Hull. Two down in seven minutes.

What a start for Newcastle United and what will really please manager Matthias Jaissle is the way both goals have come from his players winning important tackles.

The German was incensed by the lack of physicality and intensity in the heavy defeat to Leeds on Monday but the first goal for Joe Wilock came when Lewis Miley won a tackle on the edge of the Hull penalty box.

The second came when Sven Botman came away with the ball just inside his own half. On both occasions Harvey Barnes provided the assist. A short, intricate pass to Willock inside the box and then a surging, twisting run from the halfway line and the perfectly timed pass to Lewis Hall who stroked a first time shot into the bottom corner.

Hull have been outfought so far which is precisely the response Newcastle’s manager had demanded.

The home team are pressing high and all over Arsenal in the early stages. Raya has just made a save to deny Kostoulas.

Brighton have started brilliantly against the champions. They are hunting like wolves, pressing Arsenal with remarkable intensity. We have played seven minutes and I don’t think the ball has left Arsenal’s half.

Big chance for Everton to take the lead, but after great skill to turn his man at the edge of the box Brennan Johnson shoots wide with only the goalkeeper to beat.

The perfect start for Newcastle with all their injuries: Joe Willock has put the home side in a strong position against Hull with a clean strike inside three minutes.

We are under way at the Amex, St James’ Park and the Hill Dickinson.

Another famous face in the stands at Hill Dickinson Stadium today but this time it’s not about politicians. Wayne Rooney is here to watch his boyhood club and he will be hoping Everton can go into the international break unbeaten. An extra special cheer too before kick-off for Jarrad Branthwaite, who has just been called up for England duty. Plenty of Premier League clubs would like to sign Branthwaite, if they were given half a chance, but David Moyes has made it quite clear that Branthwaite: “Isn’t for sale - I want to keep my best players.”

He was not part of the match-day squad at Sunderland but Ben White’s injury has opened up a place, and Dowman fully deserves it after his two goals against Ipswich in the League Cup. Sam Dean has the story of his rise to stardom as well as what Arsenal are doing to nurture such a special talent.

Brighton are wearing a special “125 anniversary” kit today, to mark 125 years since the club was formed in 1901. It’s inspired by the colours of their first ever kit, which means an all-blue shirt, pale gold shorts and dark socks. Personally I would not allow such nonsense. But I don’t make the rules.

Spurs scored two late goals to salvage some pride against Aston Villa, but it is another defeat for Roberto De Zerbi’s team who have two points from five games. This Emi Buendia screamer put the game out of reach.

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd

It has been a term tossed around liberally at Newcastle United since Matthias Jaissle arrived as manager, but what does “vertical football” actually mean?

It is the new buzzword in football analysis, the latest fashionable phrase to describe a “new” style of football, and it has been referenced multiple times by both Jaissle and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, since the German coach’s appointment last month.

For some of us of a certain age, vertical football just seems like clever new terminology to describe an old idea.

We are getting to the stage where we really need to start asking questions about Tino Livramento’s injury record.

The right back was due to start for Newcastle against Hull City this afternoon – his first start since April – but has picked up another injury.

That will surely mean he is out of the England squad for the Nations League having also picked up a tournament-ending injury at the World Cup in the summer before the first group game.

Livramento only played 17 Premier League games for Newcastle last season, scuppering his chances of a summer move to Arsenal, missing huge chunks of the season with groin and hamstring issues.

Injuries are already cutting deep into the Newcastle squad, with four teenagers on the bench for the visit of Hull. None have played in the first team before and three of them – Michael Mills, Mason Miley and Kyrian Thompson are just 17–years-old.

Newcastle wanted a younger team this season but not this young. It was interesting to hear Matthias Jaissle talk before the game. He knows how tough this season could be with so little experience in the side.

Lewis Dunk is a surprise absentee for Brighton, it can only be because of injury, and Hurzeler has preferred Diego Gomez to the lively Yalcouye who was very threatening at Old Trafford and Coventry. He could be a handful off the bench.

Good news for Arsenal: Jurrien Timber is finally fit enough to start a match again. This is his first start since mid-March and his return is timely, given the absence of Ben White through injury. It’s also a first Premier League start for Arsenal for Bruno Guimaraes, who comes into the midfield after his impressive performance off the bench at Sunderland last weekend.

Very excited for this one today. Arsenal have won all seven of their matches so far. Only once before in their history have they won their first eight games of a season - that was in 1903, when they were playing in the Second Division as Woolwich Arsenal. pic.twitter.com/iNBxoHl4Gc

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1405. Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash

A spitting row marred the 100th Millwall-West Ham United derby and first for 14 years.

Taty Castellanos was facing trial by video after being accused of spitting on Filip Marschall during Saturday’s febrile 2-2 draw at the Den.

Millwall goalkeeper Marschall made the allegation to referee Paul Tierney, who was expected to include it in an official report that would then be assessed by the Football Association.

Spitting on an opponent is punishable with a six-match ban.

Telegraph Sport has been told West Ham striker Castellanos denies he spat on Marschall and believes he will be vindicated by video footage of the incident.

Lying little prick. Taty didn't spit ❌ pic.twitter.com/5vYxOtKqof

Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

Eleven men were also arrested at around 7.15pm on Friday on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.

The group, believed to be Millwall fans, were detained in the vicinity of a known West Ham supporters’ pub in Stratford.

Saturday’s fixture was subject to a five-mile dispersal zone, the largest ever for a football match in London, with officers granted special powers to stop and search people and vehicles without reasonable suspicion and to remove anyone causing disorder.

Riot police were out in force outside the ground, with dog units and mounted officers among 400 personnel deployed – roughly quadruple the usual number for a game there.

Those and other measures – including the use of live facial recognition, a strict segregation policy and a 12.30pm kick-off to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time – prevented a repeat of the kind of violence which has marred this fixture down the years.

West Ham fans also received a police escort to a game that saw both sets of supporters hurl foul-mouthed insults at each other throughout.

Plans to keep rival spectators apart after the match were reportedly tested by scuffles that broke out as people left the ground.

If the police were ready for a fight before the game, West Ham’s players were not as Millwall tore into them from the first whistle and dominated a first half in which they scored twice through Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli and hit the crossbar through a stunning 35-yard strike by Mark Sykes.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

However, the Championship leaders finally turned up in the second half and pulled a goal back through Mohamadou Kanté before Konstantinos Mavropanos equalised with just 10 minutes to go.

ALL SQUARE at the Den 🙌West Ham equalise in the 80th minute.Everything to play for with just 10 minutes remaining 👀 pic.twitter.com/qQmDlyuQmT

That was only after Marschall gestured that he had been spat at by Castellanos following a melee in the penalty area.

Tierney did, though, brandish a red card when Kanté pulled back Kyrell Lisbie as the substitute robbed him of the ball on the halfway line and ran clean through on goal.

The foul denied Lisbie the chance to hand Millwall their first win over their bitter rivals for 22 years, much to the frustration of fans who had roared them on from first whistle to last.

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Describing the atmosphere as “absolutely the best by far” since he joined the club almost two years ago, Neil said: “I told the players prior to the game that this game’s a real rarity and, as a player and as a manager, it’s a privilege to be part of it.”

Asked by Sky Sports for his view on the “spitting” incident, Alex Neil said: “Fil [Marschall] was saying to the referee throughout the game when that happened at that point... Obviously I’m so far away it’s hard for me to see what happened, but I wouldn’t presume that Fil would say that without cause.

“I’m sure the referee and authorities who need to deal with it will look at it and, if it warrants it, it needs dealt with and then I’m sure they will.”

"The fans are up for it, the players are up for it" 💪🏼Lyndon Dykes looks ahead to today's match, and reflects on his strong start to life as a Millwall player.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/V9nPzbh3Ob

Kevin Nolan, West Ham’s captain, was sent off early but his team-mates defied the odds to win 2-1 thanks to goals from Carlton Cole and Winston Reid either side of a stunning Liam Trotter strike.

In Millwall’s match-day squad that day were… Harry Kane and Ryan Mason.

The last time West Ham and Millwall met, Harry Kane was a Millwall player 😅This is how that game in 2012 played out 👇 pic.twitter.com/OhtVx3caCP

This rivalry was forged in different circumstances from most derby confrontations. There is none of the religious divide of Celtic and Rangers, or the politics of Barcelona against Real Madrid, or the spat over title-winning superiority of Manchester United and Liverpool. This is a tale of proximity, an internecine feud.

“There’s no politics, no nationality, nothing like that,” says Nick Hart, who hosts the weekly podcast Achtung! Millwall. “We’re very similar people, from the same backgrounds, same communities. But it’s in the Millwall supporter’s DNA for West Ham to be the ultimate rivals. Nobody else comes into the equation. You’re brought up on this stuff. It’s your history.”

Though possibly more recent history than might be suggested by the two clubs’ early foundations. The hostility that West Ham will face at the Den is no more about dockland rivalry, north-south London disputes or strike-breaking than the animosity when Manchester United visit Anfield is caused by the building of the Manchester Ship Canal.

“It really is about the hooligan era,” says a podcaster who uses the pseudonym Former West Ham Employee on the West Ham Way podcast. “The two clubs had notorious fanbases. And they grated. It came about through vying to be the No 1, battling to see who had the hardest mob. Whenever we’ve played – or even been in close proximity – things have happened.”

Jake Cooper on making the 500th appearance of his career against West Ham today! 👏Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/lTzXOwXhxd

There have only been 18 meetings between these fierce rivals since the Second World War, but absence has certainly not made the heart grow fonder. Here are some of the feud’s most notable flashpoints.

At the 1972 testimonial in honour of Harry Cripps – the renowned Millwall hard man – police horses were sent on to the pitch after West Ham supporters entered the home section at The Den. Fighting spilt over into the streets surrounding the ground.

An even bleaker turn came in 1976, when Millwall fan Ian Pratt died in a skirmish with West Ham fans at New Cross station that led to his fall under a train.

Leaflets were later handed out in the Den’s Cold Blow Lane end with a grainy picture of Pratt and a declaration in capital letters: “A West Ham fan must die next week to avenge him.”

Millwall plundered four goals on Mothering Sunday in 2004 as Tim Cahill’s double helped them to a 4-1 victory over West Ham at the Den in an incident-filled derby.

The hosts missed a penalty and had another saved by Stephen Bywater, who was later sent off. Violence followed in the stands and the match was named “The Mothers’ Day Massacre”.

Mother's Day Massacre ⏮️A 4-1 victory over The Hammers back in 2004. pic.twitter.com/TLi7xkcVJG

A hundred West Ham and Millwall supporters clashed during a screening of England’s 2006 World Cup match against Paraguay in Canada Square, which led to 16 injuries and one hospitalisation.

The clubs’ League Cup meeting in 2009 at Upton Park was listed as Category Five by police, the most serious risk of violence, and resulted in a Millwall supporter being stabbed in Priory Road, near the ground.

The Metropolitan Police said that “planned” scuffles, which involved more than 100 fans, appeared to have been caused by fans without tickets to the game.

Just spotted one Millwall fan outside the ground in blue boxing gloves. He is also wearing what appear to be slippers, so not sure what that means…

Nuno Espirito Santo has only been through the door at West Ham for a matter of months, but he insisted he is fully aware of the significance of today’s fixture.

When asked about his perception of the rivalry, Nuno said: “Since the fixture list came out, this date has been [important], for both of the clubs. It’s special, special game. We look forward to go and compete against a good team.

“It’s a different game from all of the other games, it’s a special game, the atmosphere will be different… Steve [Potts, first-team coach and former West Ham player] has been involved in many of these games, he’s constantly speaking about how special it is for West Ham fans, so we have a lot of information and we are fully aware of the importance of the game.

On potential unrest between fans and the significant police presence, Nuno added: “What we want most is that everything goes well, both fans supporting their teams and no conflict. We have people inside the club who are taking care of that. We have to focus on our tasks.”

The gaffer on tomorrow's fixture ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/6NG6t4t4Fn

#westham on the way to #millwall via #london bridge #whufc #coyi pic.twitter.com/HrWgJ6UtJY

Riot police are very much out in force outside The Den today for the 100th competitive derby between Millwall and West Ham United and first for 14 years. Dog units and mounted officers can been seen patrolling the perimeter of the ground, with 400 personnel deployed to stop violence erupting between rival fans – roughly quadruple the usual number for a fixture here. There has been no sign of any trouble with less than an hour to go before kick-off.

The game has been scheduled for 12.30pm to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time, although plenty of fans have been nursing pints before entering the ground. Other measures in place include the use of live facial recognition cameras, while a dispersal order has been imposed covering a large area around the stadium. Police were also planning to escort West Ham fans from South Bermondsey station, which will also be closed to home supporters for up to an hour after full-time. The latter measure has been deemed safer than holding the 1,800 away fans back following the game.

The Millwall-West Ham derby is one of the most notorious in English football and was most recently marred by serious violence when the sides met at Upton Park for a League Cup tie back in 2009. One man was stabbed and the match itself was interrupted on three occasions by fans invading the pitch.

Alex Neil switches out goalkeeper Max Crocombe for Filip Marschall and names the returning Mathis Servais, Kyrell Lisbie and Alfie Doughty on the bench.

Alex Neil names his Lions XI 👊 pic.twitter.com/MP0N9wMatG

Just the one change from the league leaders’ last league match as Kyle Walker-Peters comes in for the injured Joel Veltman.

Today's teamsheet 📋 pic.twitter.com/EmrxYRhsPd

"We have to quiet them down" 🤫West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen is expecting a hostile atmosphere at The Den today 🗣️Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/9tp2225Rq8

The Metropolitan Police will have 400 officers on the streets of east London for this match – about four times the norm for a Championship fixture – and it has enforced a Section 35 dispersal order in the area highlighted on the map below.

A Section 35 order authorises a Police Constable and a Police Community Support Officer in uniform to “exclude a person from an area for a period of up to 48 hours with an Inspector’s authority”.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of the highly anticipated Championship match between Millwall and West Ham United as the two clubs meet officially for the 100th time. This fixture has not been staged since 2012, and the intervening 14 years have done little to temper the ill-feeling between their passionate supporters, who will be anxious to claim bragging rights over their Dockers Derby rivals. The Metropolitan Police have placed a Section 35 dispersal order in the area surrounding The Den and will deploy 400 officers on the streets of east London.

Acrimony between the two clubs has existed since the late 19th century when Millwall Athletic, originally Rovers, battled it out against Thames Ironworks, later renamed West Ham at the Athletic and Memorial Grounds. Sixty of the two clubs’ 99 meetings came between 1899 and 1915, and while they played just seven times between 1946 and 1987, the irregularity of the game only added to its mystique, which has often spilt over into the ugly.

Both head coaches spoke at length about the significance of today’s match, with Alex Neil, in the Millwall dugout, describing it as an encounter that means “absolutely everything” but imploring his players to keep “cool heads”. His counterpart Nuno Espírito Santo revealed that he had been well advised about the game’s importance by Steve Potts, his first-team coach and former West Ham player.

Since the club’s last meeting in 2012, West Ham have ascended into the Premier League, moved into the London Stadium and won the Uefa Conference League, only falling back into England’s second tier last summer where Millwall have remained for all but two seasons. The Lions brushed maddeningly close to promotion in their last campaign as they pushed for an automatic spot until the very last weekend of the regular season before falling to Hull City in the play-off semi-finals.

Much of the pre-match talk will centre on the clubs’ long-standing rivalry, but beneath the bile and belligerence is an intriguing football match between two sides. Millwall are missing 11 first-team players and face the daunting task of stopping a West Ham side who have found their feet in the Championship, scoring 16 goals in their last four league matches.

#1404. Inside football's Christian revolution: The Premier League stars who say God has saved them from their darkest moments, stopped them diving to win penalties - and why some still face mockery and abuse for their faith

Published: 20:04 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:14 EST, 14 November 2026

When Borussia Dortmund star Felix Nmecha transferred an imaginary crown from his head onto the pitch last weekend, he probably wasn't expecting to spark a firestorm.

Arriving at the German national team camp two days later, he was summoned for a grilling by sporting director Rudi Voller and manager Jurgen Klopp. His symbol of surrender before God, a goal celebration called ‘The King’s Return’, had blown up into an international news story.

Voller, alongside many of Dortmund’s fans, was concerned by Nmecha's ties to Ballers in God, a network of Christian players founded in 2015 by former Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

While its core mission is to promote faith in Jesus, the evangelical group is believed to hold a conservative stance on issues such as sexuality and gender – a perspective Nmecha has been in hot water for promoting before.

Nmecha insisted that his message was one of love, but as his celebration was dissected worldwide, the furore posed more questions than it answered. What role does the Christian faith play for footballers? What impact is the groundswell of belief having on dressing rooms? And what should teams do when ancient creeds clash with modern culture?

For months, Daily Mail Sport has been speaking with Christian players, chaplains, and academics. We have found that some footballers are still mocked in dressing rooms for their beliefs. We have also heard tales of elite stars praying with non-League journeymen, and of faith sustaining players through injury crises and rescuing them from dark places after their retirement.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha attracted controversy in Germany for his 'The King's Return' celebration against Elversberg last Saturday

Manchester City winger Jeremy Doku is one of a growing number of practising Christians in the Premier League

For many players, their beliefs and careers are inextricable. Brentford forward Igor Thiago thinks it was part of God's plan for his father to die so that he would become a footballer and share his beliefs internationally.

'If my father were alive, I do not think I would have become a footballer, because I think he wanted me to be someone else,' Thiago tells Daily Mail Sport. 'It wasn’t until later that I understood there was a purpose for me to come here and be someone else. To be Thiago, who is a footballer, who can speak about God for so many people, in another language.'

Thiago worked as a fruit-carrier, bricklayer, and rubbish collector from the age of 13 in the streets of Gama, Brazil, to provide for his family after his dad passed away. A career in the Premier League was unimaginable back then. Now he is the main man at Brentford and one of several players at the club professing a Christian faith.

And they are not alone in their devotion. Across the top six divisions, 75 per cent of clubs have a Christian in the first team and almost half regularly host Bible studies or prayer meetings, according to a survey of 134 outfits by Christians in Sport.

Their director, Graham Daniels, remembers being told in the 1980s that he was one of just four openly practising Christians in the professional game. An impossible claim to verify, but yes, you read that right, just four. Now you have starting XIs containing more believers than that – and we hear some managers have even been attending church with their squad members. 'There’s a real movement of God within football,' one chaplain at a professional club tells us.

Perhaps God is dwelling in the treatment room, too. Bournemouth winger Ben Gannon-Doak has had three major injuries in his career – to his knee, then quad, then hamstring – and credits his growing faith for helping him recover from each blow.

'With the first, that was before I was strong in my faith – I didn't cope with that one well. I was 17 and felt lost without being on the pitch,' the 21-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport.

'The quad injury, I coped better because I started slowly practising my faith more. When my hamstring injury came, I was closer to God than I had ever been before and I coped with that very easily, it was much easier mentally than the other two. I was able to play in the World Cup after that.

Brentford forward Igor Thiago thinks it was part of God's plan for his father to die so that he would become a footballer and share his beliefs internationally

Arsenal's 'Bible Brothers' are the most famous band of Christian players – around 10 of their stars including 'pastor' Jurrien Timber (left) pray together before matches

'I believe all my injuries happened for a reason and I coped with them the way I did for a reason. I just need to trust God. It makes you stronger, prepares you for things, tests your character. It changes you. Faith has impacted my life in the best way possible.’

Multiple footballers interviewed for this piece cited the Bible verse Philippians 4:13 – 'I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me' – as a key driver in their life. Gannon-Doak has it tattooed on his left arm.

Football has always had crossover with religion – Manchester City and Everton are among the many clubs to have started as church teams, for example – but the past few years have seen it assume more public prominence.

Arsenal's 'Bible Brothers' are the most famous band of Christian players – around 10 of their stars including 'pastor' Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke pray together in the hotel before matches, and regularly share Bible verses on social media. Organisations such as F3 and Ballers in God, who hold daily prayers and weekly Bible studies, have built Christian fellowship across the divisions.

'Premier League players are on the same call with guys who are semi-pro at step four,' Omar Beckles, a player for League Two Gillingham, tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Lads got together virtually during the pandemic and have been consistently since.' But why the explosion of Christian expression now?

‘An important factor has been the increasing number of players coming from Africa or Latin America, where Pentecostalism and other forms of evangelical Christianity are strong,’ Hugh McLeod, Emeritus Professor of Church History at the University of Birmingham, explains to us.

‘Chaplains interviewed for an academic study in 2011 claimed that elite footballers had “a disproportionate passion for the faith” compared with the average member of society, and they saw the players who had come in from other continents as having a big influence on this.’

An earlier generation of Christian players graduating into management positions, as well as a broader shift in Gen Z asking the cosmic questions in life, has opened up football to the tender matters of faith. Group Bible studies, or even stoppages for Muslim players to break their Ramadan fasts, were unheard of until recent years.

'Christians in a changing room can be frowned upon,' says Steven Sessegnon, the Fulham academy graduate who now plays for AFC Wimbledon. He was mocked for being baptised

Marc Guehi was reprimanded by the FA after writing 'Jesus loves you' on Rainbow Laces armbands enforced by the Premier League in support of the LGBTQ+ community

Daniels, who is now a director at Cambridge United, says Christian values have earned players respect in the dressing room – and thinks faith could alleviate the turmoil players face when the final whistle blows on their career.

‘There was tremendous bullying in the 1980s and 1990s, but the more people saw authentic Christianity, the more they realised that it didn’t harm the changing room, but made it better,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Their integrity shone through – players felt if they talked to Christians, they wouldn’t gossip, and they’d be caring, and they wouldn’t be judgmental.

‘In football your identity is achieved. You're as good as your last game. It’s too much pressure for players. That’s why people gamble, drink, and divorce when they retire, because you spent your life having to prove yourself and you don’t know what to do with yourself when you can’t anymore.

'Or think about the academy players who are released at 16. You were the best kid in your class, then your town, your city, your region, the academy system. Then they are released and disappear from the game. Their identity is shot. They feel shame and failure for the rest of their lives.

'If you know your identity and your purpose is a received gift from God, it’s a complete contrast to everything you’ve ever imbibed. He's going to use your highs and lows in sport to draw you closer to Himself. He’s given you this vocation – this is your gift from Him and He loves you.'

Beckles concurs. ‘Being a Christian actually gives you an unfair advantage in football because you’re always living with some form of optimism and hope,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘You know there’s no despair. Setbacks are an opportunity to improve and go again. When my dad died, I really saw God show up. He granted me a level of peace and grace and joy just to function at that time when I was grieving.’

That said, there is clearly an occasional tension between faith and football, which can bring fame, wealth, and temptations untold. Pele, for example, was very open about his low-maintenance relationship with Christianity's bedroom bylaws.

Meanwhile, Daily Mail Sport has heard of stars who have felt compelled to switch church after becoming Premier League regulars as they had become too recognised and overwhelmed by their original congregation.

City star Antoine Semenyo has a close relationship with pastor John Thompson and was baptised on a beach in Bournemouth last December

Then there's the minefield of political and social issues which footballers are scrutinised over. When playing for Crystal Palace in 2024, Marc Guehi was reprimanded by the FA after writing 'I love Jesus' and 'Jesus loves you' on his Rainbow Laces captain's armband, the wearing of which was enforced by the Premier League in support of the LGBTQ+ community.

And that brings us back to Nmecha. He could have simply pointed to the sky, or made a sign of the cross, when celebrating against Elversberg last Saturday. It wasn’t his expression of faith, but rather the specific King’s Return action associated with Ballers in God, which riled a certain crowd. No matter that other players, such as Nottingham Forest's Jair Cunha, have deployed the celebration without incident. Klopp says that after their talks, Nmecha will not be repeating it. Dortmund executives will be breathing a sigh of relief.

The website for The King’s Return campaign initially linked to a live counselling chat run by conservative evangelical organisation Groundwire. There, counsellors espoused the beliefs that homosexuality is sinful and abortion is ‘Satan’s plan’. When Daily Mail Sport investigated the chat service, we were met with similar views.

It is not fully clear if Ballers in God agree with Groundwire, or if their members even assume a uniform theological position on such issues, but the network celebrated the scrapping of the Rainbow Laces initiative by the Premier League last year. They appear to have removed the link to the Groundwire chat in the wake of the Nmecha controversy. Daily Mail Sport made repeated requests for an interview with founder Bostock, who has been described as ‘hard to pin down’ and a ‘busy man’, but was turned down.

While high-profile incidents are a PR headache for clubs, there is no need for contrasting moral codes to disrupt a team’s cohesion. ‘You might not agree with someone, but you can respect them and treat them in a non-discriminatory way,’ says Dr Keith Parry, Principal Academic in Sport at Bournemouth University.

‘We’ve had openly gay players and referees at the top level in rugby. It is strange that men’s football is different, but questions around sexuality and inclusion go deeper than religion.

‘There are so many barriers (to players potentially coming out) such as toxic masculinity, fans making homophobic remarks, and so on. There are a lot of Middle Eastern and conservative North American owners in football – how might that impact on inclusion? It depends on the owner.’

Beckles, who has represented 14 clubs, believes Christian players have a duty to let love rather than division shine through. ‘Footballers are constantly in a world where there’s someone not far from them who will want something from them. Their manager and fans want them to perform, people want their signature, people want them to give them money, their agent wants commercial growth,' he tells us.

Bournemouth and Scotland star Ben Gannon-Doak (right) has the verse 'I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me' tattooed on his left arm

The young winger credits his faith with helping him through three major injuries

'It’s nice to meet someone that doesn’t want anything from them and genuinely cares for them eternally. That level of love should set people apart.'

Despite dressing rooms becoming more tolerant of faith, some players still face derision. 'Christians in a changing room can be frowned upon or mocked,' says Steven Sessegnon, a player for League One side AFC Wimbledon, who was taunted after being baptised while at a previous club.

'You hear some real nasty things. Some boys don’t understand, which we give them grace for. What scares me the most is why people get so worked up about footballers who are believers.

‘We’re not bothering anyone. We’re going about our business in a loving and caring way. It really rubs people the wrong way and it can cause arguments inside the changing room. One boy was told he will never play because he’s too soft, because he’s a Christian.'

On matchday, faith is increasingly visible and impacts how players go about their business. The temples are not always glamorous – we hear that some players have even met in the sanctuary of a broom cupboard to squeeze in prayer. Clubs offer what they can. At League One Plymouth, they take the analysis suite – at Arsenal, they have a multi-faith prayer room. Across the pyramid, prayers often ask for protection from injury and the chance to glorify God – but not for a win.

At Championship Charlton, six to eight players read the scriptures and pray together. 'They have God-given talents and want to use them as an act of worship,' says club chaplain Matt Baker, who is also on hand at the training ground on Fridays to pray with players. 'When you see players do the sign of the cross after scoring a goal, they see it as evangelistic, but it's also expressing to God that I'm doing this for you, for your glory.'

At Exeter City in League Two, chaplain George Baker tries to spread the love around the club. 'I'll do the rounds of the stadium and chat to the stewards and grounds staff,' he says. 'It's a great opportunity to value the people who are making matchday happen.’

Beckles says that religious considerations even factor on the field. 'How do you live with a level of integrity when you want to win? It’s winning in the right way. The “dark arts” are really difficult to navigate,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport, and he is not the only player to express this feeling to us.

'Being a Christian actually gives you an unfair advantage in football because you’re always living with some form of optimism and hope,' says Omar Beckles (right)

‘In my heart of hearts, I’d like to think I wouldn’t dive to win a penalty – that’s deception. I try my best not to do any of that. But there is the heat of the moment that exposes our nature.’

Gannon-Doak adds: ‘Players losing their temper, starting fights, that's the stuff I try to avoid. But some of the dark arts, that’s just part of the game.’

A popular Christian slogan since the 1890s goes as follows: ‘What would Jesus do?’ Typically it is applied to quandaries in a believer’s life – how to treat somebody who has seriously wronged you, for instance.

Not as often has it been wondered: ‘Would Jesus go down if a sweaty centre-back tugged his shirt in the penalty box in the 90th minute?’ But the next time you catch a game, you might just catch an athlete wrestling with that kind of question. What would you do?

To read more about the relationship that Brentford players have with their faith, see here.

#1403. As El Niño builds, studies of extreme marine heatwaves must start now

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alistair J. Hobday is a chief research scientist at CSIRO Environment, Hobart, Australia.

Kathryn E. Smith is a research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Claire M. Spillman is a principal research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Karen Filbee-Dexter is a Future Fellow at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and a principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Neil J. Holbrook is a professor of ocean and climate dynamics at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century, University of Tasmania, Hobart, Australia.

Caroline Rowland is head of ocean cryosphere and climate at the Met Office, Exeter, UK.

Dan A. Smale is a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Grant Smith is a senior research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Mads S. Thomsen is an adjunct professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and an associate professor in the School of Biological Sciences, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand.

Thomas Wernberg is a laureate professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Alex Sen Gupta is a professor in the Climate Change Research Centre and the Centre for Marine Science and Innovation, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia.

Coral nurseries, such as this one in French Polynesia, can be used to study the resilience of the organisms in real-world settings. Credit: Alexis Rosenfeld/Getty

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean at record-high levels and forecasts of an extreme El Niño climate event, intense marine heatwaves are expected around the world in the coming year1,2. Scientists must prepare to study these extreme conditions now, so that managers of marine resources and decision makers can develop and implement response strategies and communities can plan for a hotter future.

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

El Niño is part of a recurring natural cycle in Earth’s climate in which warmer waters in the central and eastern Pacific alter ocean and atmospheric circulation, affecting weather worldwide. Marine heatwaves associated with El Niño provide opportunities to study ecosystems under real-world stress conditions and on scales that cannot be replicated in a laboratory.

Marine heatwaves can be forecast weeks or months ahead, giving researchers time to design field studies, deploy instruments and collect baseline data. Investigations can be designed to test theories and improve our understanding of ecological processes, thresholds and recovery mechanisms in a rapidly warming ocean.

Such knowledge can inform decisions about how to manage marine resources, such as whether to close fisheries. Much has been learnt about marine heatwaves since the last El Niño, in 2023–24 (see ‘Hot water’). But these lessons need to be consolidated and scaled up into consistent, long-term preparedness plans.

Source: Climate Reanalyzer (CC-BY-4.0); go.nature.com/4zae69a

Fortunately, effective approaches established in one place can be extended to others. Australia is a leader in developing early-warning systems and response plans for adaptation to a more extreme ocean climate. Other nations (including the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Peru) have improved their awareness of these events and put in place observation systems, forecasts and briefings, policy mechanisms and (in a few cases) adaptation measures.

But further action is needed, particularly in locations that have previously been unaffected by severe marine heatwaves. Here, we highlight seven priorities in increasing marine heatwave preparedness.

Seasonal forecasts with lead times of several months are now being delivered in various regions, including the United States3 and Australia4, and such systems are being developed in the United Kingdom and New Zealand5 and for the Mediterranean Sea6.

Forecasting relies on physical and statistical models to predict probable ocean temperatures7. Data from sustained surface and below-surface observations are essential for initializing models and verifying predictions, building users’ confidence in forecasts.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

But managers want to know more precisely what the duration and intensity of a marine heatwave is expected to be. Forecasts become less accurate the further ahead they look and at fine spatial scales, such as along coasts. Improved ocean monitoring, a better understanding of the drivers of marine heatwaves and continued refinements of model physics are needed to improve forecast accuracy7.

Advances in machine learning are expected to be transformative. Next-generation models that incorporate ocean physics might be able to predict unprecedented marine heatwaves more accurately than current technologies can. Downscaling global climate models to inshore regions using machine-learning techniques could also increase the usefulness of forecasts in places where most marine-resource users operate.

Planning for and communication about impending marine heatwaves are also improving1. In 2023, engagement was piecemeal and often only in response to events that were already in progress. Activities are now more proactive and structured.

Coordinated briefings that translate forecasts into action provide ways of engaging with affected groups and planning ahead. Such communication strategies should be implemented around the world4,8. National briefings provide a broad overview of marine heatwave risks and impacts. Regional and industry specialists can provide further local advice.

For example, Australia’s national marine climate briefing series4 has been running since 2023. Similar meetings (led or contributed to by some of us) have taken place for the western Pacific Ocean (G.S.) and in the United Kingdom (C.R.), Brazil (K.E.S.), Singapore (C.M.S.) and New Zealand (C.M.S.).

Seafood-producing firms and conservation managers need a menu of actions to choose from when a marine heatwave looms. Options include adjusting collection strategies, temporarily closing fisheries and modifying aquaculture operations1.

Australia has developed regional and industry-specific response plans for marine heatwaves8. Response teams for fisheries are active during warming events and provide coordinated mechanisms for assessment, communication and management actions4,9.

Impacts of marine heatwaves are being monitored in restored giant kelp forests in Tasmania, Australia.Credit: Scott Ling/University of Tasmania

Early-warning systems and interagency coordination are key components of timely responses. Industry has also adopted operating protocols to reduce the impacts of marine heatwaves on animal health and food-product quality. For example, abalone fisheries in New South Wales have changed how sea snails (Haliotis spp.) are fished, handled and prepared for live export10. Other regions could benefit from similar plans4.

For example, fishing of Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens), the source of around 20% of fishmeal and fish oil globally, has already been curbed by the current El Niño. In 2023, the fishery had to be closed, resulting in an estimated loss11 of US$1.4 billion. This year, an alert in February prompted Peruvian authorities to bring the fishing season forwards by two weeks and reduce the total allowable catch of anchoveta and white anchovy (Anchoa nasus) by more than 30% to 1.9 million tonnes. This meant that fisheries could catch about 450,000 tonnes before the heatwave intensified and the season was ended in May.

In 2023, marine heatwave preparedness was recognized as inadequate in most regions. The emphasis then was mainly on raising risk awareness in sectors such as fisheries and aquaculture1. However, these and other industries need to adapt to a changing ocean, too.

Awareness has now grown among sectors and institutions, and behaviours have begun to change. For example, Australian marine climate briefings draw engagement from aquaculture and fishery managers, marine tourism operators, policymakers, researchers and individual fishers4.

In the United States, forecasts of marine heatwaves trigger advice to fishers regarding increases in interactions with marine mammals as the overlap between animals’ hunting grounds and deployed fishing gear expands, which can result in fishery closures. Coral-reef managers involved in restoration efforts can scale back replanting efforts and start collecting genetic material.

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

In the Mediterranean Sea, limiting diving tourism at coral reefs to minimize damage during marine heatwaves has been proposed, mirroring practices that were adopted in Asia during the 2023–24 marine heatwaves11.

In the Cook Islands’ black-pearl industry, seasonal forecasts have been proposed for supporting decisions around adaptive management aimed at reducing the thermal stress of oysters. These include increased reliance on hatchery production under controlled temperature conditions and preferential harvesting of pearls during cooler periods of the year.

In the United Kingdom, a national marine heatwave network and code of best practice have been established, enabling the exchange of transdisciplinary knowledge. Similar transfers of experience, capacity and lessons learnt between jurisdictions can accelerate preparedness globally and help to embed risk management into routine decision-making processes4.

The 2023 El Niño led to calls to strengthen monitoring and research capacity to improve the detection of, understanding of and response to marine heatwaves. Observation networks are now becoming a core component of preparedness and response plans, providing the information needed to support forecasting, impact assessment, management interventions and long-term adaptation strategies12.

Targeted uses of gliders and intensified monitoring strategies can bolster research, situational awareness and management decisions12. Research has expanded into understanding ecological resilience and adaptation. For example, genetic studies are identifying traits that might enhance the capacity of key fishery or habitat-forming species13 to persist under increasing thermal stress.

Researchers in Florida are studying corals obtained from local reefs as part of restoration efforts.Credit: Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare
