Harry Kane is scheduled to hold a press conference after the match at Wembley to talk about the achievement of joining Peter Shilton on 125 caps.

Secret to Harry Kane’s England longevity? ‘He strikes the ball better than Ronaldo’

Right foot, goal. Left foot, goal. Edge of the area, goal. Inside the area, goal. Under pressure, goal, Right foot, save. Left foot, goal. That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Myles Lewis-Skelly is expected to get a recall to the team after playing against Czech Republic in Prague last week when England won 2-0. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.

Probable England team: Pickford; Trent, Quansah, Guehi, Hall; Lewis-Skelly, Anderson; Rogers, Bellingham, Eze; Kane

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

Shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

England played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

In the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. He will have to find replacements for the injured Alex Scott and Ezri Konsa, however, and Calvert Lewin, who has had seven minutes of action, Rio Ngumoha 19, Morgan Gibbs-White 27 and Jarrad Branthwaite one, may feel they deserve a fairer opportunity to show what they can do in a match.

#1374. Guimaraes looks a £75m bargain as ‘super sub’ makes difference

Arsenal have played six Premier League games this season and Bruno Guimarães has been a match-winning force in two of them. At this rate, he might justify his enormous £75m transfer fee by Christmas.

The Brazilian was not signed to be Arsenal’s super sub but that is the role he appears to be playing in these early days in north London. Against Leeds United here, as it was against Sunderland last month, he came off the bench when the champions were struggling. And as it was at Sunderland, he produced a thumping finish to put Arsenal on their way to three points.

This is the value of signing a 28-year-old with significant Premier League experience. As Arsenal laboured against an impressively organised and courageous Leeds side, Mikel Arteta knew that Guimarães was capable of coming into the game and adjusting to its demands. There has been no adaptation period required for Guimarães, who is fast becoming one of the most popular players in north London.

The finish, which put Arsenal 2-1 ahead at the Emirates Stadium, marked an emphatic conclusion to a fabulous passing sequence. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Declan Rice all combined at speed before Guimarães charged on to Rice’s flick. “It was a beauty,” said Arteta of the goal. The move had actually begun at the feet of Guimarães a few moments earlier, when he nutmegged an opponent in style.

The winning goal came just eight minutes after Riccardo Calafiori, Arsenal’s thrilling left-back/centre-forward hybrid, had pulled them level in the game. James Justin had struck for Leeds shortly after half-time, creating a horrible anxiety among the home fans here, and for much of the afternoon Daniel Farke’s side were the better team.

Leeds finally have their opener! 🤩 James Justin arrives at the back post to fire them ahead. 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/ITjUMSlrG1

Leeds, though, could not compete with Arsenal for depth. The arrival of Guimarães as a 63rd-minute substitute represented a flexing of Arteta’s managerial muscle, in his first match since signing a new long-term contract, and the Brazilian offered a moment of attacking quality that his opponents were unable to replicate.

It was actually the first competitive home game that Guimarães had played for Arsenal since his transfer from Newcastle United, as a result of a few niggles and the club’s unusual run of four consecutive away matches before the international break. The most recent of those was the 3-0 thrashing by Brighton, which was one of their worst defeats of the last few seasons.

This gritty victory represented a necessary response to that defeat, even if the performance was far from dominant. “We had a point to prove,” said Arteta. “Something was touched in our identity against Brighton.”

Guimarães, too, clearly felt that some wrongs needed to be made right. For all his brilliance in this game and against Sunderland, he had produced a horrible showing at the Amex Stadium a few weeks ago. “He was not at that level against Brighton,” said Arteta. “This is the level for Arsenal. Every week, every game, every minute, every action you have to be at that level. At Brighton, he wasn’t. Today, he was much better.”

Leeds had not lost in their opening five Premier League matches of this season and it was easy to see why. They were willing to press Arsenal high up the pitch, taking risks and engaging in physical duels, and the strategy proved hugely effective for an hour.

If they had been more precise in the final third, they could have been a few goals ahead by the time Justin converted Gabriel Gudmundsson’s left-wing cross after 55 minutes. Anton Stach, who was accidentally blocked by team-mate Jayden Bogle, and Gudmundsson both went close in the first half.

The early kick-off, the long international break, the slow start and the memories of the Brighton defeat made it a strange atmosphere at the Emirates. You would not have known they were the champions, based on the reaction of the fans to the first-half performance, but the achievements of last season clearly do not guarantee fervent support at all times.

Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall believes Thierno Barry's impressive form for Everton is the product of relentless work to improve his game behind the scenes.

Barry has notched 13 goal involvements (10 goals, three assists) in all competitions so far this season, most recently a quick-fire brace in the Blues' 3-1 come-from-behind victory over Coventry City prior to the international break.

The French striker also produced the assist for Dewsbury-Hall's goal against Frank Lampard's side – and it comes as no surprise to the Toffees' No.8 to see his teammate thriving.

"Cream always rises [to the top] when you work hard. I'm a big believer in that.

"I know he'll keep working, keep a level head and I think he'll keep getting better and better, because he's got the right attitude."

Dewsbury-Hall has also praised the collective mentality of Everton this season.

#1372. OLIVER HOLT: Why England CAN now end 62 years of hurt - Thomas Tuchel is intoxicating and I'd tip Jude Bellingham to beat Kylian Mbappe to the next Ballon d'Or... plus my top 10 Three Lions performances

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026

The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning. ‘Fin a la racha,’ the headline said. The end of the run.

For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.

For England, the feeling was very different. Because Sunday night in the cauldron of the Metropolitano felt very much like a beginning. Thomas Tuchel has been the head coach for almost two years but this was the moment of his true arrival.

This was the victory that freed us from looking back to the Groundhog Day pain of that World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in Atlanta last summer and allowed us to look forward to a future that seems luminous and full of hope.

This was the victory that allowed us to stop blaming Tuchel for what happened four months ago and start looking forwards again, dreaming about the glories that he might yet deliver. This was the victory that validated Tuchel and why the FA hired him in the first place. This was the victory that allowed us to believe he might be the Messiah after all.

This felt like the moment when he embraced us, with all our quirks and football idiosyncrasies, and we embraced him. He had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it with bells on. Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game and welded it to his principles and the result is intoxicating.

Thomas Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game to down world champions Spain

Once you have seen England play the way they did for an hour against Spain, you are lost. You are lost to the belief that the 62 years of hurt might really be coming to an end at Wembley in the final of the European Championship in the summer of 2028. You are lost to the idea that, finally, everything is falling into place.

For the 63 minutes up until the sending off of Elliot Anderson, I have never seen an England performance as good as the one that unfolded in the Metropolitano. Spain are the best team in the world and England outclassed them and stupefied them. They were better than them with the ball and better than them without the ball. They were magnificent.

Because of the context, because of the wonder of the stage, because of the odds they faced, England’s victory over Mexico in the grandeur and the mayhem of the mighty Azteca Stadium during the World Cup might edge Sunday’s performance but for pure football, what England delivered in Madrid demands comparison with the best they have played for many a year.

This year’s World Cup came just too soon but now Tuchel and England understand each other perfectly. And now England are purring. They have a manager who commands the players’ respect and they have a group of players that commands the respect of the manager.

Yes, it was just a Nations League group game but it was against one of the best national sides the world has ever seen. England worked so ferociously and attacked so fluently and defended so devotedly that they reached a level that drew admiration even from their opponents.

Many, many things will live long in the memory. James Trafford’s miraculous double save in the dying minutes gets better every time I watch it. Ben White’s goal channels the beauty of Carlos Alberto’s strike for Brazil against Italy in the 1970 World Cup Final, too. Let’s hope that strike, and his superb defensive performance, bring an end to the boos that have been his companion of late.

Jude Bellingham was relentless, tireless and glided through the game against Spain

Tuchel had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it

And then there was Jude Bellingham. Just when you think you can’t admire him any more than you do, he delivers a performance like the one he produced against Spain, a performance that lifted him above even the exalted company of the other players on two fine teams.

Bellingham was tireless. He was relentless. He glided past challenges. He thundered into tackles. He dominated midfield. He has the heart and the sheer brilliant indomitability that Bryan Robson possessed.

Bellingham has it in him to be England’s greatest ever player. He needs trophies to fulfil that destiny but maybe, finally, trophies are in reach again.

He has the team around him to do it, which Robson never quite had. Jordan Pickford is a good goalkeeper but Trafford might just be better. Ezri Konsa had his best game for England in Spain. White and Lewis Hall were superb at full back. Little more needs to be said about England’s front six. They are as good as any unit in world football.

Harry Kane, of course, was the best player in the world last year. Some seem to assume that the Ballon d’Or will inevitably pass to Yamal or Kylian Mbappe next. I think it is more likely to be Bellingham.

The man is a colossus. He is a footballer who has everything. He does not know how to be beaten.

Bellingham saw off Barcelona rival Lamine Yamal - and could beat him to the Ballon d'Or

With them together, the sky is the limit. And Bellingham has also proved to be a player of immense mental strength. It was not so long ago that people worried about his discipline but the fortitude he showed when he was being targeted by Argentina at the World Cup was the best answer to that.

He and Kane are England’s axis of ambition on the pitch. Tuchel is lucky to have them and they are lucky to have him, too. The coach has reached the point where his tactics and his team-building are bearing fruit.

Now England have a team-manager package that genuinely need fear nobody. The victory against Spain was a rehearsal for the bigger stage of major tournaments. Going down to 10 men after 63 minutes against the best team in the world might not have been in the script but that is what rehearsals are for.

After Sunday night in the Metropolitano, England are ready for their close-up.

#1370. New US Congress should ‘reimagine’ science — not just return to the past

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Kenneth M. Evans is a fellow in science and technology policy at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, Houston, Texas.

The results of the US midterm elections will bring changes in Congress that could affect how science is governed.Credit: Aaron E. Martinez/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty

The US Democratic Party’s sweeping victory, which saw the party take electoral majorities in both chambers of the US Congress, has rekindled optimism in the science community over the future of the nation’s research system.

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Science advocacy organizations and members of Congress are now rushing to address scientists’ most pressing question: how much money will be allocated to research in the spending bill for the fiscal year 2027?

When it convenes on 3 January, the 120th Congress should also address two thornier, longer-term questions: who should get to participate in making decisions about science and technology? And how can policy institutions adapt to include more public voices?

These questions sit at the centre of science’s ‘social contract’, the government-led support system that exchanges taxpayer funding and scientific autonomy for the promise of downstream public benefit. And they speak to a much older problem than the Second World War-era debates that created the modern US research system: the challenges of how to govern and the role of experts in democracies.

In the main, postwar US science policy has privileged experts over the public. In the 80 years since the publication of science adviser Vannevar Bush’s report Science, The Endless Frontier, the government has tested policy mechanisms that more closely align science with the nation’s social and economic needs. But public engagement remains in the wings.

Entire NSF science advisory board fired by Trump administration

Entire NSF science advisory board fired by Trump administration

The National Science Foundation (NSF), a major funder of basic science at universities, has grown to embody the US social contract. And it has become a battleground for the competing visions of academia and the White House over federal science policy.

With no Senate-confirmed director and its acting director due to leave at the end of the year, the NSF faces a widening leadership gap. The American Institute of Physics and others have reported in detail on the firing, in April, of the National Science Board, which helps to oversee the NSF. Agency observers say that the absence of a Senate-confirmed director has made the NSF subject to greater White House direction.

The agency awarded nearly 50% fewer grants in the 2026 fiscal year than in the years from 2021 to 2024. The NSF has said that it has carried over more than $1 billion into the 2027 fiscal year to invest in agency priorities aligned with broader initiatives of the administration of President Donald Trump. It has two years to spend its research appropriations, although it does not typically carry over such a large share of its annual budget.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has overhauled the nation’s long-standing social contract with science and, with it, the trusted partnership between universities and the federal government. The resulting impact on US science and increasing public attention on science policy has opened a unique window for reform. Congress should seize this opportunity to reimagine the nation’s science-policy institutions, rather than just trying to stitch them back together.

#1369. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1367. ‘Light and sound’ therapy for Alzheimer’s flops in long-anticipated trial

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Asher Mullard is a science journalist based in Ottawa.

The Spectris AD headset produces flashing lights and sounds designed to induce gamma waves in the brain.Credit: Cognito Therapeutics

A device that uses flickering light and rhythmic clicking sounds to stimulate the brain failed to slow memory loss in people with Alzheimer’s disease, according to results from a highly anticipated clinical trial.

The device, called Spectris AD, consists of goggles paired with headphones that individuals wear for an hour a day at home. The flickering light-and-sound show is designed to induce brain activity called gamma waves, which have been linked to increased attention and memory.

But after a year of treatment, participants who used the device did not show any improvement in their cognitive function compared with those assigned to a sham treatment. The results were reported by US medical-technology firm Cognito Therapeutics, which makes the device, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease meeting held in Boston, Massachusetts, on 16 November.

Although disappointed by the results, Christian Howell, Cognito’s chief executive, said that the results show beneficial signs for people with mild cognitive impairment. The company plans to file for approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) next year, he adds.

“The effect that we saw in the mild subgroup was so meaningful,” Howell said. “It just gives us optimism as we move forwards.”

But researchers are not convinced. “The trial was negative,” says Eric McDade, a neurologist at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. “If anything is going to happen after this, it should be a follow-up study in that mild population,” he says.

In the trial, 673 people with Alzheimer’s disease were randomly assigned to use either an active or a sham Spectris AD device for 60 minutes a day for 12 months. After the year, those who used the active device scored, on average, 8.97 points less on a 156-point scale that measured cognition and ability to perform daily activities than they did before using the device. The scores of participants who used the sham device declined by 8.82 points.

Can flashing lights stall Alzheimer’s? What the science shows

Can flashing lights stall Alzheimer’s? What the science shows

Howell says that the device was more effective in people with mild, rather than moderate, cognitive impairment. In the mild-impairment group, active-device users experienced 42% slower decline than sham-device users — a difference of three points on average.

For Rob Howard, a psychiatrist at University College London who specializes in dementia, these data are exploratory rather than a persuasive proof of efficacy.

“If this was a drug, such a clear failure would mean that a company would not proceed to seek regulatory approval,” says Howard. The safety of the device doesn’t make it any more useful to patients, he adds.

Previous trials of Spectris AD haven’t panned out either, adds Howard. In 2024, a smaller trial of the device failed to slow the decline of cognitive and functional abilities in people with Alzheimer’s disease1.

The results are a setback for researchers who have been working to understand how gamma brain-wave modulation could bolster brain health.

#1366. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

News breaks that City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.

Telegraph Sport understands that Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur were contacted in advance of the email to the other 15 clubs.

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

It is the most unlikely Oasis song title for a banner but, in a sea of canvas, the word will jump out from the Kop: Acquiesce.

The simplest flags frequently carry the most profound messages and, on a red background, below Acquiesce is the declaration: “MCFC Cheats”. It has been prepared specially and specifically for the return of domestic football to Anfield.

Given the tone coming out of the Etihad Stadium, nobody will be acquiescing to any alleged wrongdoing, certainly not on Sunday, but minds were made up on Merseyside about how far City had pushed the boundaries in pursuit of success a long time ago.

“There has been a lot of talk about various things,” explains John Gibbons, host of Anfield Wrap, the popular Liverpool podcast. “Manchester City trying to say they are going to be hard done to, but there are no great surprises among Liverpool fans about these charges, are there?

“Everyone who goes to the match, who supports Liverpool, have known all along that a lot of those sponsorship deals looked questionable. Did they pass the smell test? That’s why the atmospheres in the past when City came were always brilliant and I’m expecting it will be the same again.”

So that is why Anfield will be a maelstrom of sound and fury for one of the most significant occasions in Premier League history.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1365. My Everton #180: My Mind Was Made Up For Good

I was born in North Wales in 1980, and my first memory of football was playing for the school team as a kid.

As a nine or 10-year-old I started getting my cousin’s hand-me-down Everton shirts, and this certainly helped me decide which of the local sides I was going to follow!

The two red sides close by (Wrexham and the other lot) never once turned my head.

And then, in 1991, my mind was made up for good. My uncle asked me if I’d like to go to watch Everton play.

It was the first ever game I’d been to watch live. It was at Bramall Lane, and I’ll never ever forget it.

My uncle got us to the ground early and took me and my cousin to wait for the players’ coach to turn up.

The coach arrived and as I was only a little kid at that point, my uncle lifted me up to get a glimpse of the players.

The first player I saw was big Neville Southall and I reached over to pat him on the back and wish him good luck. He glanced over his shoulder and gave me a wry smile.

Not only was I now hooked on Everton, but all I wanted to be from that point on was a goalkeeper.

A few years later I got to taste my first ever trophy win as an Evertonian. Me and my dad watched the whole FA Cup final build-up from Grandstand in the morning to Match of the Day, with the game in between.

We couldn’t get tickets to the final, but my uncle and cousin did go the Charity Shield.

Even though that was my last taste of silverware as an Evertonian, my love for this club has never wavered.

I’m now 46 years old, lived in Australia for 20 years and I’m happily married with seven children – six of which have all been to Goodison and the youngest has beat me to visit the new stadium last year!

-              - 1995 and the FA Cup victory

-              - Going to Howard’s testimonial a few months before leaving for Australia

-              - Spending a day painting parts of Goodison in 2013

-              - Goodison trips with my dad, cousins, uncle and taking my six kids to see the eventual champions in 2016

-              -Taking my two sons to the games in Sydney

-              - My daughter (who now lives in Rochdale) going to the last game at Goodison

-              - And my wife taking our two youngest daughters to see our stone at the new ground last year.

I’ve got so many fond memories of our beautiful club, and I can’t wait to make millions more in the coming decades.

There is no other football club for me or my family. Once a Blue, always a Blue

#1363. Is academia’s risk-averse culture stifling scientific discovery?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Nessa Carey's career has straddled both academia and industry. “In industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams,” she says.

Academia, on the other hand, is more personality-driven, and feels more individualistic. “Failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal,” she adds.

But as global research collaborations become more multidisciplinary, a culture change is needed in higher education, says Carey, who now runs a training business that supports biotechnology and drug discovery spinoffs.

Earlier this year, Carey spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the penultimate episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Carey urges academia to look at how industry handles failure, where struggling projects are abandoned more quickly.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03772-y

Is innovation as slow as it's often labelled?

Oftentimes we talk about innovation being slow, but in fact, you know, many of us feel like we're living in an ever-changing society.

After the failure and innovation session, the chair, Dr Nejra van Zalk, a design psychologist at Imperial College London, reported back to delegates attending the Failure in Science Conference, held in April this year.

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

Why do we choose innovation in one area of healthcare, for example, and not in another area? And who makes those decisions?

Why do we focus on obesity drugs and pump money into that, rather than helping to fix musculoskeletal issues in children who would have much better outcomes over a lifetime.

I'm Dr Stephen Webster, director of The Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don't.

And in episode five of this series, we explore the business of discovery.

To put it bluntly, when it comes to failure, could universities learn a thing or two from industry?

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

How can we safely incorporate failure into our working models?

Can we look to industry to see how they're doing it when they actually, they cut their losses sooner and they abandon projects quicker and they can quantify their risks in different ways than we can in academia.

So my name is Nessa Carey, I'm a PhD scientist. And I've worked in academia, in industry, and as a freelancer. So I've kind of done a lot of things over the space of my career.

Oh, so so many failures. I started out with the classic academic failures of having grants rejected, having papers rejected.

In industry, you get things like programmes that you simply can't keep running. And also if you move to industry, you will be made redundant at some point or another.

And it's very easy, particularly the first time, to view that as a personal failure, but as you get more experienced, you realize it's just about organizations, it's just about shifting priorities, and actually it's not that big a deal.

So your definition of failure changes as your career changes. And also as you get older, I think it changes as well.

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

I wanted to ask us, and perhaps ask the panel: as society, and this is not simply a UK perspective I don't think, have we become hyper risk averse?

Is that the direction that we're heading in?

And if so, where is the space for failure, and particularly the space for failure in science?

So, in the opening session of the conference at Imperial College, Professor Jem Woods suggested that we have become too risk averse and that that has really negative consequences, for example in academia.

And I think I absolutely agree with that, but I don't think it's just academia that is negatively impacted by this.

And I think the conversation has shifted, and not necessarily in a way that's helpful. And I think it's particularly a lot of pressure on younger people.

So I do quite a lot of outreach work in schools, and I see young students who are under enormous pressure to do well at their GCSEs or their A levels or whatever is the equivalent in another country, because they have to get onto the right course at the right college. They have to get a career trajectory that's working in the right direction.

And so I think there's a much bigger fear of failure because the stakes have been made artificially high.

In reality, as long as you do a course that you're happy on at a university where you're happy living, you'll do fine.

But we've built in this terrible sequential success demand on the young, and I think it's also exacerbated by [the fact we] we now have much more public discourse because we have social media, and everybody posts their triumphs. Everybody posts their success. You look at LinkedIn, and it's just full of people celebrating their promotion, their latest certificate, etc.

The trouble is that's not real. That's not how life generally progresses. You try stuff, you stuff up, you learn from it, and you move on.

And if we always class that as failure rather than a normal part of learning, then I think we do create really, really big problems for the future because everybody will try and stay inside their comfort zone.

Everybody will be frightened of doing something wrong.

It's a big problem in science because science thrives on innovation, but it's a big problem in any creative sector, and we run the risk of situations where people would rather do nothing than take a risk.

And you see that in organizations as well, and that's a really big problem.

I think what academia could do with learning from industry in terms of failure is to depersonalize it somewhat.

I think that's extremely difficult to do in reality.

One of the things that I enjoyed about working in industry, as opposed to working in academia, is in industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams. And yes, you may be the leader of a team, but you're still a team.

Academia, I find generally is much more individualistic.

If you have a much more individualistic environment, it is much harder to acknowledge failure as being simply a consequence of good decisions that are made by a team.

In academia, failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal. And it's very personal, in particular, to the Principal Investigators.

In industry, you can be doing really interesting work on a project, and then you do the killer experiment and realize your project can't go anywhere. And as a team, and as the leader of a team, you make the decision that that project needs to be terminated.

Now, that in academia would feel like failure because you can't then go on and apply for grants for it.

In industry, there's much more an emphasis in good companies on “did we make the right decision?”, and if you made the right decision, then the target failed or the program failed, but you didn't necessarily fail as an individual.

And I think it's that difference between viewing things as projects and teams and viewing things as individual endeavours.

And given that more and more science is becoming multidisciplinary, multi-team, it would make so much more sense if academia could start to change its culture towards that, because on the whole, the big papers that we see coming out now – they're big team efforts, and yet reward still tends to remain very individual.

So it's a structural issue. It's not just about people.

I think academia could adapt well by adopting some of the good managerial and people development skills of industry.

Academia is, in my experience, much more driven by personalities, and that creates enormous emotional heft behind things.

In industry, of course, there are big personalities. There are in every sector, but because you're working as an organization, you don't have quite this same strange mix of your personal emotional life with your professional life, and so you can fail professionally without it having quite the same impact on you as an individual emotionally, if that makes sense.

Something that the industry has got very, very good on is identifying killer experiments, carrying them out, and doing the thing that is considered a cliche now – but is absolutely critical – of fail fast, fail quickly, fail early, fail cheaply: that you don't keep trying to progress something that cannot get to the end point that you need.

And I think industry, on the whole, is very good at that. It used to be very bad. It's got better.

Academia is terrible at that in my experience, in that what will happen is somebody has their favourite target, their favourite process, their favourite enzyme, and they just keep working on it because they have a reputation for that and because they can keep working on it, rather than thinking “do you know what? It'd be really good to set up this experiment, see if I'm on the right track, and if I'm not, I'll kill it.” Instead, what they tend to do is just find other things they can keep working on in the same field.

Now, sometimes that's entirely appropriate, and sometimes it's that real curiosity-led stuff that takes us in a weird direction and opens up all sorts of things.

But there is always a risk that you will just keep chugging away at something because you know you'll at least get a couple of papers out of it, or because your PhD student needs the data for their thesis, etc.

It's a very different environment, and so it's not that I'm saying we should import everything from industry into academia, but I do think sometimes academia could benefit from the critical thinking of industry that goes: take away the emotion and actually look at this from scratch and say, “would we carry on if we were starting now?”

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

So I mentioned these grand challenges; We often talk about them in science circles, The grand challenges. What's the role of science in helping society address these grand challenges?

And the emergence of innovation in technologies, I think has now switched to hyper disruptive technologies, and that's specifically around how we manage, or [how] information is managed. (When I say we, maybe it's not managed).

And then societal and community and individual access to those innovations in technology, and I think it's often labelled as ‘The BBC's Post-Truth Society’, because there were many of the BBC journalists (and some of them may be in the audience I don't know) who talked a lot about this emergence of that technological system in the post-truth society. And we have real questions in science to answer around that understanding of the way that information is generated and the way it's perceived and used societally.

So, in the opening session, Jem Woods was talking about the fact that there's been a drop of trust in science, and I wouldn't say it's just science.

There's a drop in trust in multiple areas, including in our trust in politicians, and our trust in writers, and our trust in the media.

And I think it's phenomenally important that scientists continue to do their work to the highest level of probity, and the vast majority of scientists do that, and that is true whatever sector you're in.

Scientists are remarkably similar, whether they're in academia or they're in industry; they're there because they want to do good science.

I think it's vital that everybody continues to do really good science. I think it's also vital, though, that we do challenge one another appropriately and professionally.

But what is also really important is that scientists continue to communicate, to a wider public, what is important about science and the scientific method, and also to be very upfront about the limitations of our research and the limitations of our findings.

This again, I think, ties into the issue of success and failure, because one of the things that's happened is public engagement and communication of science have been added to the academic workload.

The academic workload never decreases; new stuff always gets added to it, and it becomes another box to tick.

And there is a risk that people not only need to do good science, but they need to do science that can be communicated well.

And I think the most dangerous thing for academia is that it's constantly under pressure to justify why its science is being done. What is the benefit, the direct, very tangible benefit for humanity?

And that creates pressure to overstate one's outcomes, to be too black and white about it because black and white stories sell – it's much easier to sell a black and white story – but we have to be really careful not to do that because every time we do that and get challenged, we undermine the faith not so much in our science, because each member of the public has probably forgotten us, but the faith in science itself.

We shouldn't be scared of saying it's complicated, and so I think there is a real risk there that by being unsubtle about how we communicate our science, we actually undermine faith in a field which has essentially added enormous benefit to humanity and to the planet, and we need to be very careful not to lose that.

So I've worked in the field of innovation for about 25 years, and it's just as difficult now as it was 25 years ago.

But I think there are particular issues now that we're facing as a world that we didn't face back then. AI is the obvious one of having created a technology that actually may outrun us, and no one's quite clear how that's going to play out now.

But I think there are bigger issues at stake here as well.

I think it's very difficult when so much science is being published and being done to work out which of it genuinely has the potential to shift the needle on a particular issue.

But I think it's actually at risk of us having such a focus on innovation, in the sense of ‘where's the next great widget? Where's the next great drug?’, that we forget that technological innovation may not actually be what we require to solve particular problems.

So one of the things that really really frustrates me is seeing more and more emphasis, and more and more funding, in climate change going into carbon capture.

Carbon capture at scale is an entirely unproven technology, and it's not clear at all that it can solve the climate change problem.

We do, however, know that moving to electric cars makes a huge difference, and yet we are not in the UK legislating to do that appropriately.

We also have a situation where drug companies are spending billions of dollars to develop drugs for chronic health conditions that we actually know are caused essentially by social inequality and poverty.

We would be so much better as societies if we would put our money into more equitable healthcare systems, more equitable food availability systems.

We would have an enormous return on investment, but we don't see that return on investment for a very long time, and it's not a capitalist return on investment, it's a government return on investment.

So my concern is that our biggest failures will come because we constantly try to ‘tech’ our way out of problems that don't actually require technological solutions.

They require different, longer-term, less glossy solutions that don't make money for companies, and our systems on the whole run in a way that have placed an awful lot of, say, healthcare and environmental responsibilities and opportunities on big capitalist companies, when actually they are not the right structure to deliver those outcomes.

So that is where I think our biggest failures will come: We will ‘tech’ when we shouldn't be ‘tech-ing’. We will try and ‘tech’ very expensively when actually we could have made smaller investments with much more impact.

And it is deeply frustrating to me that also we as scientists will go “don't worry, we'll come up with a technological solution.” instead of saying “we may never come up with a technological solution, but if you talk to our friends in the social sciences, they already know what needs to be done. Why on earth aren't you doing this?” And that, I think, is a failure on the part of science to pretend that we are the ones who will solve everything.

#1362. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE

In a flash the balance of play shifted in Newcastle’s favour. They poured forward in search of the equaliser. Jaissle switched to a 4-4-2 with Will Osula joining Fernandez-Pardo up front, but instead of pulling level, Coventry pulled further ahead.

"We need to improve the things we can control, and right now that's a lot" 🗣️ Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle expresses his disappointment after his side's loss to Coventry 👇 https://t.co/fatJkZYyRM

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. We know we are going to have to suffer this season, when we don’t have a lot of the ball. We have to understand it. The level is what it is.

The work ethic, the belief. You get what you deserve. Great finishes. We haven’t quite had the rub of the green this season and that might have helped us nick a couple of more points. I’m a firm believer that you keep going. It was a complete performance. We’ve got to keep our feet on the ground because we’re going to have to do 30+ of those but it’s a great feeling for the players.

[Cherif] is very, very exciting because he is so young. He has got a really good manner. He wants to train, he wants to learn. He’s quite quiet but on the pitch he shows a lot of personality. When you see the quality of the strike and the hold-up play, there’s a lot to come from him.

"That one was for you, nan" Jack Rudoni explains his goal celebration ❤️ https://t.co/79OvHMlu6J

A victory to savour for Coventry whose teenagers Cherif and Mfuni scored fine goals. No doubt they wobbled when Botman equalised and for the next 10 minutes but Newcastle blew too many chances and resumed making errors at the back. Newcastle’s squad is a mess.

Newcastle might maintain that Thomas-Asante was offside and blocking the keeper’s view when Mfuni pulled the trigger but I think Hornicke had a clear view and hence it wasn’t an offence.

The first two minutes of stoppage time, of which there are four, pass without incident.

Osula lifts a volley over the bar with a wild attempt. Toure was injured in the build-up and will be replaced by Dan Burn.

Never mind Bob Gelodof and Brenda Ann Spencer, Matthias Jaissle doesn’t like Mondays. They are 8-2 down on Monday Night Football so far this season.

Coventry 4 Newcastle 1 (Mfuni) The substitute had only just replaced Rudoni and took the ball on the inside-left 25 yards out, advanced then wrapped his instep around a left-foot shot, arrowing it across Hornicek into the bottom right.

Stephen Mfuni makes his mark for Coventry! 👊 https://t.co/KI2kgpfUJP

Thomas-Asante crashes a right-foot shot into the heart of the left post. A thumping strike that leaves the metalwork ringing.

Coventry 3 Newcastle 1 (Simms) Right foot shot from 18 yards through Thiaw’s legs, clipping the inside of his right knee to deflect it into the bottom left. Joelinton had been trying to dribble it out of the box, overhit it and fouled Thomas-Asante as he tried to recover. The whistle was betweeen the ref’s lips but he did not exhale as Simms steered his shot through Thiaw’s legs.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

Touré beats Dasilva for pace down the right then blazes over from a tight angle then moments later is given an opportunity to shoot and sticks it in the stands again. Both times the cross was on.

Toure has caused untold problems for Dasilva. Newcastle corner on the left is bent far too deep and goes out for a goal-kick.

Wissa dithers over a shot when found by Toure to the right of the penalty spot and finally clips it into Thomas. Coventry are clinging on but flapping. As is the crowd.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”
